⚖️ Her Flogging, His Offering — Linked by One Verse — the guilt offering depends entirely on whether she is flogged
😴 Exemptions: Forbidden Relations vs. the Maidservant Case — minors, sleepers, and unwitting actors compared
🔀 Rav Sheshet Untangles a Confusing Baraita — a garbled teaching about typical/atypical intercourse gets sorted out
🧀 Witnesses and the Sin Offering for Forbidden Fat — a new mishna maps out testimony, contradiction, and silence

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing the Maidservant Chapter, Opening Testimony
overview.subtitle: Keritot 11a–11b
overview.hebrewSource: בִּזְמַן שֶׁהָאִשָּׁה לוֹקָה – הָאִישׁ מֵבִיא קׇרְבָּן, אֵין הָאִשָּׁה לוֹקָה – אֵין הָאִישׁ מֵבִיא קׇרְבָּן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by pinning down exactly who qualifies as the 'espoused maidservant' of the mishna — a dispute stretching across several tanna'im about whether she must be half-slave, half-free, or simply a full maidservant betrothed to a Hebrew slave. The Gemara then derives, from the order of a single verse, that the man's liability to a guilt offering is entirely contingent on whether the woman herself is flogged, and works through a new mishna's list of exemptions (minor, sleeping, unwitting) that apply differently in this case than in every other forbidden relation. A confusing baraita about typical and atypical intercourse gets carefully untangled by Rav Sheshet. The chapter then closes, and a fresh mishna opens tractate Keritot's discussion of testimony: how witnesses' statements — consistent, split, or contradicted — determine whether a sin offering or a provisional guilt offering is owed.

slides.title: 🤷 Who Is the 'Espoused Maidservant'?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's key term draws several competing readings
rows: Half-maidservant, half-free woman — owned by two masters, one of whom freed his share; 'redeemed and not redeemed' (Lev. 19:20) is read literally
A full-fledged Canaanite maidservant; the doubled phrase is just idiomatic Torah speech ('the Torah speaks in the language of people')
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov / Rabbi Akiva
All other forbidden relations are fully enumerated; the maidservant case is the sole 'exception' — specifically a half-slave betrothed to a Hebrew slave
A Canaanite maidservant betrothed to a Canaanite slave — derived from 'they shall not be put to death because she was not free'

callout.label: Supporting text:
callout.text: Rav Ḥisda cites Ezra 10:18–19, where priests married 'foreign women' and brought guilt offerings, as proof that guilt offerings apply specifically to relations with an espoused maidservant.

slides.title: ⚖️ Her Flogging, His Offering — Linked by One Verse
slides.subtitle: The Gemara derives this dependency from the verse's word order

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'There shall be an inspection (בִּקּוֹרֶת תִּהְיֶה)' — the feminine form תִּהְיֶה teaches she alone is flogged, not him

2️⃣ The verse places 'there shall be an inspection' before 'he shall bring his guilt offering' — teaching that his liability depends on hers: if she is flogged, he brings an offering; if not, he does not
3️⃣ Could she still be flogged even when he brings no offering? No — 'he shall bring his guilt offering' specifies only him, never her
4️⃣ Rabbi Yitzḥak adds a further limit: he is liable only for a non-virgin maidservant (נֶחֱרֶפֶת, 'designated' — a term implying she has already 'changed' status)

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Unlike ordinary forbidden relations, where man and woman face parallel liability, the maidservant case makes the man's offering wholly derivative of her own punishment.

slides.title: 😴 Exemptions: Forbidden Relations vs. the Maidservant Case
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: the same exemption categories apply very differently here

boxes.title: All other forbidden relations
items: Sleeping partner exempt; awake partner still liable
Unwitting brings a sin offering; intentional brings karet — two distinct tracks

boxes.title: The maidservant case
items: If either partner is a minor, both are exempt — their liabilities are 'juxtaposed to each other' in the verse
If either partner is asleep, both are exempt — same juxtaposition logic
Liability is entirely linked: no independent track for the man

callout.label: Rav Yehuda's key move:
callout.text: He reinterprets the mishna's opening clauses: 'minor exempt' and 'sleeping exempt' in the general case implicitly means 'the adult/awake partner is liable' — a contrast the maidservant clause then overturns entirely.

slides.title: 🔀 Rav Sheshet Untangles a Confusing Baraita
slides.subtitle: A baraita seems to equate opposite categories — is it corrupted?

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: 'They equated completion with initial stage, intentional with unintentional, typical with atypical, awake with asleep' — but this seems backward for the maidservant case!

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Should I strike this baraita as corrupted? None of these equations make sense for either the maidservant case or ordinary forbidden relations.

lines.speaker: Rav Sheshet
lines.text: No — keep it. It means: atypical completion with a maidservant (exempt) is equated to typical initial-stage contact (also exempt) — both fail the verse's requirement of 'lies carnally' (שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע, seed-bearing intercourse).

lines.speaker: Rav Sheshet
lines.text: Likewise: intentional-but-atypical is equated to unintentional; awake-but-atypical is equated to asleep — all four pairs share the same underlying exemption, atypical intercourse.

callout.label: Net effect:
callout.text: Every atypical-intercourse scenario with a maidservant collapses into the same exemption category as the most obviously exempt scenarios among ordinary forbidden relations.

slides.title: 🧀 Witnesses and the Sin Offering for Forbidden Fat
slides.subtitle: The new mishna opening the next major topic: testimony and liability

nodes.content: 👥 Two witnesses say 'you ate forbidden fat' and he stays silent → liable to a sin offering
⚖️ One witness says 'he ate,' another says 'he did not' (or two women split) → uncertain → provisional guilt offering
🙅 One witness says 'he ate,' and he himself denies it → exempt — his denial overrides a lone witness
🤔 Two witnesses say 'he ate,' and he denies it → Rabbi Meir: liable (a fortiori from the graver penalty of death); the Rabbis: exempt, since he might have meant 'I did it intentionally'
🍽️ Separate stringency: eating different forbidden foods (fat, blood, piggul, notar) in one lapse → liable for each; eating the same food twice in one lapse → only one offering

callout.label: Torah source for liability despite testimony:
callout.text: 'Or if his sin is known to him' (Lev. 4:28) teaches that being informed by others — not only self-discovery — creates liability for a sin offering, provided he does not contradict them.

summary.principle: The espoused maidservant's case ties every element of liability — the definition of the woman herself, the man's offering, and every exemption — directly to her own status and punishment, in sharp contrast to ordinary forbidden relations where each partner's liability stands independently; and the new mishna on testimony shows liability for a sin offering likewise depends precisely on how witnesses' words interact with the sinner's own.

flowSteps.content: 🤷 Tanna'im dispute whether the maidservant is half-slave/half-free or a full maidservant betrothed to a Hebrew or Canaanite slave
⚖️ The verse's word order makes the man's guilt offering entirely dependent on the woman being flogged
😴 Minor/sleeping exemptions apply jointly to both partners in the maidservant case, unlike ordinary forbidden relations

columns.content: 🔀 A garbled-looking baraita in fact equates every atypical-intercourse scenario with clear exemptions elsewhere
🧀 A new mishna maps witness testimony (consistent, split, denied) to sin offering, provisional guilt offering, or exemption

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability tracks precisely how the Torah's text links (or separates) two parties' statuses, and precisely how testimony does or does not survive contradiction

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda, who qualifies as the 'espoused maidservant' discussed in the mishna?
o: Any fully free woman
A woman who is half-maidservant and half-free, owned by two masters one of whom freed his share
Any gentile woman regardless of status
A widow who remarried
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda reads 'redeemed and not redeemed' (Leviticus 19:20) literally, defining the espoused maidservant as a woman partially freed — half-maidservant, half-free.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's derivation from the verse's word order, what determines whether the man brings a guilt offering for relations with an espoused maidservant?
o: His own intent alone
Whether the woman herself is flogged — if she is not flogged, he brings no offering
The season of the year
Whether he is married
quiz.e: Because 'there shall be an inspection' (her flogging) is written before 'he shall bring his guilt offering,' the Gemara derives that his liability to an offering depends entirely on whether she is flogged.

quiz.q: In the maidservant case, what happens according to the mishna if one partner is a minor or one partner is asleep?
o: Only the minor or sleeping partner is exempt; the other remains liable, as in ordinary forbidden relations
Both partners are exempt entirely, since their liabilities are juxtaposed to one another in the verse
Both partners are always liable regardless of age or wakefulness
The law is silent on this scenario
quiz.e: Unlike ordinary forbidden relations (where only the minor or sleeping partner is exempt while the other remains liable), the maidservant case links both partners' liability together, so a minor or sleeping partner on either side exempts both.

quiz.q: According to Rav Sheshet's explanation of the seemingly corrupted baraita, what does 'they equated completion with the initial stage' mean with regard to the maidservant?
o: Both are always liable
Atypical (non-procreative) completed intercourse is exempt, just as typical initial-stage contact is exempt — both fail to meet 'lies carnally' (seed-bearing intercourse)
The baraita is meaningless and should be deleted
Completion always creates liability regardless of manner
quiz.e: Rav Sheshet explains the baraita is not corrupted: it equates atypical (non-procreative) completed intercourse, which is exempt, with typical initial-stage contact, which is also exempt — both fail the Torah's requirement of 'lies carnally.'

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is the outcome if one witness says a person ate forbidden fat, and the person himself denies it?
o: He is liable to a sin offering
He is liable to a provisional guilt offering
He is exempt entirely, since his own denial overrides a single witness
He receives lashes
quiz.e: The mishna rules that when a single witness's testimony is directly contradicted by the person's own denial, he is exempt — a lone witness's word does not override his own statement.
